extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism/media studies; journalism professionals and instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria about how individual journalists' characteristics, professional roles, and ethical frameworks shape news content; includes codes of ethics (SPJ), conceptions of professionalism, and role typologies (interpretive/dissemination/adversary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion coverage scope and criticality
rubrics_metrics.description: The news media give less emphasis to covering religion than other institutions; there are few full-time religion editors and religion beats are often treated as peripheral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect uneven and sometimes uncritical coverage of religious news; reporters often 'suspend critical judgment' on paranormal/religious-interest stories. Evaluate stories for whether they present skeptical voices or investigators (e.g., James Randi) and whether both sides are represented; anti-patterns include quoting only believers or misquoting skeptics and treating religion beats as marginal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias must appear in the copy to matter
rubrics_metrics.description: "Bias that counts must be in the copy, not just in the minds of those who write it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating bias, look for evidence in published content (selection of sources, framing, language), not merely presumed private attitudes. Search text for systematic slant in how actors/events are described or omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worldview influence on news judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists' 'worldviews'—their perceptions of social reality—influence news judgment: decisions about sources, news pegs, and language will partly reflect how a journalist perceives and understands the social world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess stories for implicit value-laden choices (who is covered, what is ignored, descriptive language). Guidance: examine what is reported/ignored and how actors/activities are described to detect values 'between the lines.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional role — Interpretive function
rubrics_metrics.description: The interpretive function: investigating official claims, analyzing complex problems, and discussing national policy (identified as the dominant professional role for modern U.S. journalists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate reporting on whether it probes official claims, provides analysis of complex issues, and situates events in policy context. Note that >60% of surveyed journalists scored high on this scale in Weaver & Wilhoit (1983).

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional role — Dissemination function
rubrics_metrics.description: The dissemination function: getting information to the public quickly and concentrating on the widest audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess timeliness, brevity, and broad-audience orientation. Recognize trade-offs: speed and reach can limit depth or analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional role — Adversary function
rubrics_metrics.description: The adversary function: serving as an adversary of government or business (a relatively minor role among surveyed journalists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether reporting acts as an independent check on power (investigative/adversarial coverage). Expect fewer journalists to prioritize this role; print journalists more likely than broadcast to value it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profession criterion: full-time occupation
rubrics_metrics.description: A profession is characterized by being a full-time occupation; many journalists do work full-time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as one indicator when determining 'professional' status, but not sufficient alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profession criterion: deep commitment to professional goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are deeply committed to the goals of the profession (journalists are probably less committed than physicians).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess degree of long-term commitment to journalistic ideals and public service as a marker of professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profession criterion: governance by formal organization with standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Entrance to and continuance in the profession are governed by a formal organization that has established professional standards (note: journalism lacks an enforceable licensing authority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate presence and enforcement of institutional standards, codes of conduct, and formal oversight; absence weakens claims of 'profession' status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profession criterion: prescribed schooling and specialized body of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are admitted following prescribed formal schooling and acquisition of a specialized body of knowledge (journalism lacks a single prescribed body of knowledge or required degree).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider educational requirements and standardized curricula as markers of professionalization; variability across programs reduces uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profession criterion: must serve society
rubrics_metrics.description: A profession must serve society; news media serve society by transmitting information, providing context, socializing members, and entertaining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge work partly by its public-service value (information, accountability, context) rather than solely commercial aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profession criterion: high degree of autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Members must have a high degree of autonomy (journalists face organizational constraints that limit autonomy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess level of editorial independence from management, owners, advertisers, or sources; autonomy affects ability to follow professional norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Socialization to organizational norms (Breed)
rubrics_metrics.description: New journalists learn rights, obligations, norms, and what the organization wants by observation, editing feedback, and 'osmosis' rather than direct instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating practice, account for informal learning channels (editing deletions, gossip, supervisors' silence) that convey policy; these shape accepted behaviors and content choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational constraints vs individual values
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizational routines and constraints may negate the influence of individual journalists' attitudes, values, and beliefs; the power of organizational routines varies across organizations and is probably inversely related to individual influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how newsroom routines, policies, and institutional pressures (time, resources, corporate policy) limit or shape individual journalists' ability to reflect personal values in content.

rubrics_metrics.name: SPJ Code — I. Responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The public's right to know of events of public importance is the overriding mission; journalists who use their status for selfish motives violate a high trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether reporting serves the general welfare and avoids exploiting professional status for private gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: SPJ Code — II. Freedom of the Press
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom of the press is an inalienable right and must be guarded; it carries the freedom and responsibility to discuss, question, and challenge government and institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether journalism upholds the right to speak unpopular opinions and the privilege to dissent while exercising responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: SPJ Code — III. Ethics (conflicts of interest and professional conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must be free of obligation to any interest other than the public's right to know. Specific prohibitions/requirements: avoid gifts/favors/free travel/special privileges; avoid secondary employment/political involvement/holding public office/community service if it compromises integrity; avoid activities that create real or apparent conflicts; do not publish private 'news communications' without substantiation; seek news that serves public interest; protect confidential sources; plagiarism is dishonest and unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these items to evaluate conflicts of interest and personal conduct. Examples: do not accept valuable gifts, avoid political candidacy or PR work, require substantiation before publishing private-source claims, and maintain source confidentiality where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: SPJ Code — IV. Accuracy and Objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Good faith with the public is foundational. Subpoints: truth is the ultimate goal; objectivity is a performance standard to strive for; no excuse for inaccuracies or lack of thoroughness; headlines/photos/telecasts should be warranted and not out of context; distinguish news reports from opinion; partisanship that departs from truth violates journalism spirit; provide informed analysis and label advocacy pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate factual accuracy, thoroughness of reporting, contextual integrity of visuals/headlines, clear separation of news vs opinion, and labeling of advocacy or interpretive pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: SPJ Code — V. Fair Play
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must show respect for dignity, privacy, rights, and well-being. Subpoints: do not communicate unofficial charges affecting reputation without chance to reply; guard against invading privacy; do not pander to morbid curiosity; promptly and completely correct errors; be accountable and encourage public grievances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether subjects were given opportunity to respond, whether private matters were unnecessarily exposed, timeliness and completeness of corrections, and openness to audience feedback and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: SPJ Code — VI. Mutual Trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Adherence to the code is intended to preserve mutual trust between journalists and the public; the Society will encourage adherence via education and encourage outlets to frame codes with employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate practices in light of fostering trust: existence of training, published standards, and organizational commitment to codes of ethics.
